shortDef: 10-step cytoplasmic pathway converting glucose to 2 pyruvate, net +2 ATP and +2 NADH.
Mitochondrial 8-step cycle that fully oxidises acetyl-CoA, yielding 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP + 2 CO₂ per turn.
The cell's universal energy currency. Hydrolysis releases ~-30.5 kJ/mol.
Reduced form of NAD+. Donates electrons to Complex I (~2.5 ATP each).
Reduced form of FAD. Donates electrons to Complex II (~1.5 ATP each).
Substrate concentration at which v = Vmax/2; inverse measure of enzyme affinity.
Maximum reaction rate when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate.
1/v vs 1/[S] plot — linearises Michaelis-Menten kinetics; y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = -1/Km.
Inhibitor competes with substrate at active site. Vmax unchanged; apparent Km increased.
Inhibitor binds an allosteric site. Km unchanged; Vmax decreased.
Inhibitor binds only the ES complex. Both Km and Vmax decrease proportionally.
Glycolytic enzyme (step 1). Low Km (~0.1 mM), ubiquitous, product-inhibited by G6P.
Liver/β-cell isoenzyme. High Km (~10 mM), kicks in only at high glucose.
Rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis (step 3). Activated by AMP and F2,6BP; inhibited by ATP and citrate.
Glycolysis step 10. Substrate-level phosphorylation; PEP → pyruvate + ATP. Activated by F1,6BP.
Multi-enzyme complex converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. Needs B1, B2, B3, B5, lipoic acid.
TCA step 1: acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate. Inhibited by ATP, citrate, NADH, succinyl-CoA.
TCA rate-limiting enzyme (step 3). Produces NADH and CO₂. Activated by ADP, Ca²⁺.
TCA step 6, AND Complex II of the ETC. Produces FADH₂.
Muscle → lactate → liver → glucose → back to muscle. Liver pays the ATP cost of resynthesis.
Hepatic glucose synthesis from non-carbohydrate precursors. Bypasses the 3 irreversible glycolysis steps. Costs 6 ATP.
Animal storage polysaccharide. α-1,4 main chain with α-1,6 branches every 8-12 residues.
Plant storage polysaccharide. Amylose (linear α-1,4) + amylopectin (α-1,4 with α-1,6 branches every 24-30).
Plant structural polysaccharide. β-1,4 glucose linkages. Humans lack β-glucosidase — dietary fibre.
Glucose-α-1,2β-fructose. Non-reducing (both anomeric carbons locked).
Galactose-β-1,4-glucose. Reducing disaccharide. Hydrolysed by lactase.
Glucose-α-1,4-glucose. Reducing disaccharide from starch hydrolysis.
g of I₂ absorbed by 100 g fat. Measures unsaturation.
mg KOH to saponify 1 g of fat. Higher = shorter chains.
Most abundant membrane phospholipid; major lung surfactant component.
Sterol lipid. Membrane fluidity regulator and precursor to steroid hormones, bile acids, vitamin D.
Rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Target of statins.
Drug class that competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, lowering cholesterol synthesis and serum LDL.
9 AAs that cannot be synthesised: Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Leu, Lys (PVT TIM HALL).
Molecule with both + and − charge, net neutral. Amino acids at physiological pH.
pH at which net charge = 0. Proteins are least soluble at pI.
Amide bond between α-COOH and α-NH₂ of two amino acids. Planar, partial double-bond character, restricted rotation.
Right-handed coil, 3.6 residues per turn. H-bonds between residue i and i+4.
Extended strands H-bonded side-by-side. Parallel or antiparallel.
Covalent bond between two cysteine -SH groups. Stabilises tertiary structure. Reduced by DTT or β-ME.
Loss of higher-order structure with primary structure intact. By heat, urea, detergents, reducing agents.
Apoenzyme + cofactor — catalytically active enzyme.
Enzyme protein without its cofactor. Inactive.
Organic cofactor, usually vitamin-derived (NAD+, FAD, CoA, TPP, PLP, biotin, B12).
Inactive precursor activated by limited proteolysis. Examples: pepsinogen, trypsinogen, clotting factors.
Regulation by a molecule binding away from the active site. Often sigmoidal kinetics.
Different proteins catalysing the same reaction. Example: LDH-1 to LDH-5.
4-digit Enzyme Commission number. First digit = class (1 oxidoreductase, 2 transferase, 3 hydrolase, 4 lyase, 5 isomerase, 6 ligase).
Double-stranded antiparallel helix with deoxyribose sugar. Stores genetic information.
Usually single-stranded with ribose sugar and U (instead of T). mRNA, tRNA, rRNA — many roles.
Carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes for translation.
Adaptor that carries amino acids to ribosomes; reads codons via anticodon.
Structural and catalytic component of ribosomes.
3-nucleotide unit in mRNA coding for one amino acid (or stop). 64 codons → 20 AAs + 3 stops.
AUG. Codes for methionine and initiates translation.
UAA (ochre), UAG (amber), UGA (opal). Terminate translation.
Flexibility in 3rd codon base position; explains code degeneracy.
DNA → RNA → Protein. Plus self-replication (DNA → DNA) and reverse transcription (RNA → DNA).
Enzyme that copies DNA. Has 5'→3' polymerase and 3'→5' proofreading activities.
Enzyme that transcribes DNA into RNA. Bacterial version is rifampicin's target.
Antibacterial that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase. First-line TB drug.
Antibacterials that inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase / topoisomerase IV. Example: ciprofloxacin.
4-complex system in inner mitochondrial membrane that transfers electrons to O₂ while pumping H+.
ATP synthesis driven by the H+ gradient established by the ETC. Mitchell's chemiosmosis.
ETC entry point for NADH. Pumps 4 H+ per electron pair. Inhibited by rotenone.
Final ETC complex. Reduces O₂ to H₂O. Inhibited by CN⁻, CO, azide.
Rotary motor in inner mitochondrial membrane. Uses H+ flow to make ATP from ADP + Pi.
Lipid-soluble mobile electron carrier between Complexes I/II and III.
Small water-soluble heme protein. Shuttles electrons between Complexes III and IV.
Mitchell's 1961 proposal that the H+ gradient drives ATP synthesis. Nobel 1978.
Molecule that ferries H+ back across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. Energy → heat.
Disorder of glucose homeostasis. T1: no insulin (autoimmune). T2: insulin resistance.
β-cell hormone. Lowers blood glucose by stimulating uptake and storage; suppresses gluconeogenesis.
α-cell hormone. Raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase. Treated by low-Phe diet.
Hyperuricemia → MSU crystal deposition in joints. Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase.
Xanthine oxidase inhibitor used in gout. Suicide inhibitor — oxidised to oxypurinol in situ.
Mitochondrial pathway breaking down fatty acids to acetyl-CoA, with FADH₂ and NADH yields per round.
System (CPT-I, CPT-II) that transports long-chain fatty acyl-CoA into mitochondria. Inhibited by malonyl-CoA.
Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone. Made by liver during fasting, ketosis, DKA.
Hepatic 5-enzyme cycle converting NH₃ to urea. Defects cause hyperammonemia.
Transfer of an α-amino group between an amino acid and an α-keto acid. PLP (B6)-dependent.
Removal of an α-amino group as NH₃, often via glutamate dehydrogenase.
Transaminase. Elevated in hepatic, cardiac, muscle injury.
Transaminase. Liver-specific; elevated in hepatocellular injury.
Hydrolase. Elevated in bone (Paget's, growth) and cholestatic liver disease.
Hydrolase that breaks down acetylcholine at synapse. Target of neostigmine, organophosphates.
Isomerase that manages DNA supercoiling. Bacterial version = quinolone target. Eukaryotic II = etoposide, doxorubicin target.
Folate analogue. Competitive inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase. Anti-cancer, anti-rheumatic.
Inhibitor of Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). Causes lactic acidosis and death.
Vitamin B12 precursor. Cyanide antidote — sequesters CN⁻ as cyanocobalamin.
Vitamin B1 → TPP cofactor for PDH, α-KG DH, transketolase. Deficiency: beriberi, Wernicke.
Vitamin B2 → FAD, FMN. Deficiency: glossitis, cheilosis.
Vitamin B3 → NAD+, NADP+. Deficiency: pellagra (3 D's).
Vitamin B5 → Coenzyme A.
Vitamin B6 → PLP cofactor for transaminases, decarboxylases.
Vitamin B9 → THF. One-carbon transfer for purine and dTMP synthesis. Deficiency: megaloblastic anemia.
Vitamin B12 — cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
Vitamin B7 — cofactor for carboxylases (pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase).
Fat-soluble vitamin. Cofactor for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X. Warfarin antagonist.
Fat-soluble vitamin. Vision (retinal), epithelial integrity, gene expression (retinoic acid).
Fat-soluble vitamin. Calcium and phosphate homeostasis. Active form is 1,25-(OH)₂-D₃.
Fat-soluble vitamin. Major lipid-phase antioxidant.
Insulin-responsive glucose transporter in muscle and adipose. Translocates to membrane on insulin signal.
Refilling TCA intermediates drained for biosynthesis. Major: pyruvate carboxylase.
Cytoplasmic pathway. Generates NADPH (for biosynthesis, antioxidant defence) and ribose-5-P.
Rate-limiting PPP enzyme. Most common enzymopathy. Deficiency causes drug- or fava-bean-induced haemolysis.
Reducing power for biosynthesis (fatty acids, cholesterol) and maintaining reduced glutathione.
Pyruvate ↔ lactate. Tissue-specific isoenzymes used as biomarkers (LDH-1 cardiac, LDH-5 liver).
Ranking of how much a food raises blood glucose after eating. Pure glucose = 100.
Non-enzymatic glycation of haemoglobin β-chain N-terminus. Diagnostic marker for diabetes; reflects mean glucose over ~3 months.
Glycogenesis enzyme. Adds α-1,4 glucose units to glycogen. Activated by insulin, inhibited by phosphorylation.
Glycogenolysis enzyme. Releases glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen ends. Activated by glucagon/epinephrine.
Ligase that converts pyruvate to OAA. Anaplerotic and gluconeogenic. Biotin cofactor.
Gluconeogenesis enzyme. OAA → PEP with GTP. Induced by glucagon.
Gluconeogenesis enzyme that bypasses PFK-1. Inhibited by AMP and F2,6BP.
ER-bound liver enzyme that produces free glucose. Liver-specific; muscle lacks it.
Single-ring nitrogenous base. Cytosine, Uracil, Thymine. Mnemonic: CUT the Py.
Two-ring nitrogenous base. Adenine, Guanine.
X-linked HGPRT deficiency. Severe juvenile gout + neurologic features (self-mutilation).
Ligase that charges tRNA with its specific amino acid using ATP. One per amino acid.
Protein-RNA machine for translation. Bacterial 70S (30S+50S); eukaryotic 80S (40S+60S).
Equilibrium dissociation constant for an inhibitor-enzyme complex. Lower Ki = tighter binding.
